title: Tenant spend quota enforcement with granular accelerator preference and graceful model-variant fallback
creator: Ava Martin
description:
Problem statement: Customers running multi-tenant workloads need predictable monthly/weekly spend caps and graceful degradation when quotas are reached. Current routing supports region/tier preference and spot vs on-demand selection but lacks a real-time enforcement layer that understands tenant-level spend headroom, fractional GPU allocation (bin-packing to improve utilization), and controlled model-variant degradations (to cheaper quantized variants) when spend thresholds approach.

Goal: Implement a routing policy and enforcement shim that: 1) tracks per-tenant spend in short windows (1m/1h/24h) with token-level estimated cost, 2) enforces soft and hard spend gates that trigger model variant fallback or request throttling, 3) prefers specific accelerator classes per-tenant with fallbacks (e.g., prefer A100, allow T4 if cost constraints), and 4) supports fractional GPU allocations for small requests to increase packing efficiency without violating latency SLOs.

Requirements / Acceptance criteria:
- Real-time spend accounting accuracy within +/-10% for short windows using token cost heuristics and cached per-model per-sequence estimators.
- Soft gate behavior: when headroom < 10% recommend/automatically route to cheaper variant or spot GPUs, emit reason codes and tenant-facing telemetry.
- Hard gate behavior: when headroom exhausted, either (a) reject with explicit quota-exceeded error, or (b) fall back to a pre-authorized free-tier model variant depending on tenant policy.
- Configurable tenant policy surface: monthly cap, emergency buffer, preferred accelerator list with weights, fallback model variants and ordered fallbacks, and notification hooks.
- No regression to latency SLOs for P95 requests in production more than +10% relative to baseline for requests not routed to cheaper variants.

Design (high level):
1) Spend accounting collector: extend token-metering pipeline to emit per-tenant provisional cost events into an in-memory time-windowed store (sliding 1m/1h/24h buckets). Use amortized token cost estimates per model variant and per GPU class multiplier (spot discount factor). Persist periodic snapshots to billing metrics backend for reconciliation.
2) Routing policy engine: new policy plugin that evaluates (tenant policy, current headroom, region capacity, accelerator preference) and produces an ordered list of candidate endpoints with actions: ROUTE, FALLBACK_TO_VARIANT, THROTTLE, REJECT. Prioritize endpoints by expected unit cost adjusted for latency impact score.
3) Fractional GPU allocator: lightweight allocator that aggregates small requests across tenants into micro-batches bound to fractional NUMA slices or a multi-tenant slot on the same physical GPU where memory/KV cache isolation is possible. Introduce admission controls to prevent tail latency amplification.
4) Enforcement shim (ingress): intercept incoming requests, consult the policy engine and provisional spend store, attach routing decision metadata (reason_code, estimated_cost, chosen_variant), and call the router. For soft gates, attach a ‘notice’ header and emit a telemetry event.

Tradeoffs and considerations:
- Accuracy vs performance: keeping accounting in-memory gives low-latency decisions but requires reconciliation to avoid drift. We accept small periodic reconciliation adjustments rather than synchronous billing checks.
- Fractional GPU complexity: packing increases efficiency but adds KV cache compaction and potential cross-tenant interference; to mitigate, only enable fractional packing for models with compact KV footprints and for tenants with explicit opt-in policy.
- Spot evictions: when spot instances are evicted mid-request, fallback policies must be swift; prefer model-variant fallback (quantized on-demand) for long-running sequences.

Telemetry and observability:
- New events: spend_window.update, routing.decision, fallback.invoked, quota.soft_warning, quota.hard_reject, fractional_pack.success, fractional_pack.latency_penalty.
- Dashboards: per-tenant spend headroom timeline, soft/gate violation rates, fraction of requests served by fallback variants, latency breakdown for fractional-packing routes.

Rollout plan:
- Phase 1 (canary): opt-in tenants only, soft warnings emitted, no hard rejections. Validate accounting accuracy using reconciliation with billing backend for 2 weeks. UX: Console shows predicted headroom and simulation toggle.
- Phase 2 (graduated): introduce soft automatic fallbacks for selected tenants and model variants (configurable). Monitor latency and quality regressions.
- Phase 3 (enforced): enable hard gating for low-risk tenants with email/sms notifications and customer-specified emergency buffers.

APIs and Configs:
- Tenant policy config fields: monthly_cap, window_policy (1m/1h/24h thresholds), preferred_accelerators (ordered list), fallback_variants (ordered list of model ids), fractional_pack_opt_in (bool), emergency_buffer_pct.
- New SDK header x-redwood-quota-policy to surface chosen behaviors for debugging.

Test plan:
- Unit tests for spend accounting with synthetic token streams.
- Integration tests simulating spot eviction and validating immediate fallback.
- Load test verifying P95 latency impact for fractional packing under mixed workloads.
- E2E canary with 5 customers covering small bursty, long-seq, and steady traffic.

Open questions / blockers:
- Billing team needs to expose a low-latency read API for historical reconciliation. (Blocker: BILL-AP-17)
- Product decision: default behavior on hard cap—reject vs fall back to free-tier variant. Need PM input.
- Security: ensure fractional packing does not leak cross-tenant state (security review required).

Next steps / action items:
- Diego to prototype the policy plugin and spend collector (spike: 3 days).
- Ava to draft the tenant policy schema and console mocks.
- Request BILLING to provide reconciliation read endpoint (ticket created).
- Schedule security review with platform security (target 2025-03-08).
